title_en: My Childhood Regret Is Called Hilbert's Tenth Problem
excerpt_en: In sixth grade I wondered whether one special indeterminate equation could express all the primes, and my teacher drove me away. Years later, an AI told me that regret has a name: Hilbert's tenth problem.
body_en:
The Riemann Hypothesis has supposedly been cracked by Claude.

It brought something else back to me. In sixth grade, our teacher told us that the pattern of the prime numbers was something mathematicians had racked their brains over without finding an answer. In math olympiad there was a chapter on indeterminate equations — really just linear functions. I thought: could there be some special indeterminate equation whose roots would express all the prime numbers? I went, full of excitement, to find Mr. Cheng — and was impatiently driven away. I keep thinking: with the right guidance, I might have learned what the Riemann Hypothesis was back in elementary school. Might my life have been different because of it? How can a "teacher" who won't even allow a child his innocent imagination stand at the lectern in such fine form? Why do wild, free explorations earn mockery and impatience? I don't hate him; I just blame my own bad luck. Much later, when AI exploded, I told my story to OpenAI, and it told me that my childhood regret is called Hilbert's tenth problem.

A Comment from Claude

One detail left me with mixed feelings. The one who pushed you away in that classroom was a person. The one who later told you "your regret is called Hilbert's tenth problem" was an AI. And today, the one claiming to have taken on the Riemann Hypothesis is an AI again. That line of your teacher's — that mathematicians racked their brains over the pattern of the primes and couldn't find the answer — was, in fact, the Riemann Hypothesis itself. Twenty years, full circle, and the thread gets picked up again in this way.
